body:
Why Plants Need Nutrition

Every living organism needs energy and materials to maintain its cells, grow, repair damaged structures and carry out essential life processes. The process by which an organism obtains nutrients and uses them for these functions is called nutrition.

Plants differ from animals in an important way. Most green plants can manufacture their own organic food from simple inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide and water. Animals and fungi generally depend on organic food already prepared by other organisms.

Autotrophic and Heterotrophic Nutrition

Autotrophic nutrition is a mode of nutrition in which an organism prepares organic food from simple inorganic substances using an energy source. Green plants generally use sunlight as that energy source.

The word autotrophic means self-nourishing. Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria are examples of organisms that perform photosynthetic autotrophic nutrition. Organisms that depend on ready-made organic food are called heterotrophs. Humans, other animals and fungi are familiar examples.

Plants do not obtain their main supply of carbohydrates by absorbing ready-made food from the soil. They manufacture these carbohydrates themselves. Soil mainly supplies water and mineral nutrients necessary for their growth and metabolism.

What Is Photosynthesis?

Photosynthesis is the process by which chlorophyll-containing organisms capture light energy and use it to manufacture carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen during oxygenic photosynthesis.

In ordinary green plants, photosynthesis takes place mainly in the leaves. The green pigment chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which is converted into chemical energy and ultimately stored in organic compounds.

Requirements and Products

  • Carbon dioxide: Supplies the carbon used to manufacture carbohydrates. It normally enters leaves from the atmosphere.
  • Water: Supplies material required in photosynthesis. In terrestrial plants, it is generally absorbed from the soil by roots.
  • Sunlight: Provides the energy that drives the process.
  • Chlorophyll: Absorbs light energy required for photosynthesis.
  • Carbohydrates: Represent the food manufactured by the plant. Glucose is a familiar example, and surplus carbohydrates may be converted into starch for storage.
  • Oxygen: Is released during photosynthesis and can diffuse from the plant into its surroundings.

The simplified overall equation is:

\(6CO_2+6H_2O\xrightarrow{\text{light}}C_6H_{12}O_6+6O_2\)

Chlorophyll absorbs the light required for the reaction. This equation summarises the overall process rather than every intermediate reaction taking place inside the plant.

What Happens to the Manufactured Food?

The carbohydrates produced during photosynthesis have several uses. Some are broken down during cellular respiration to release energy for plant activities. Some are used to manufacture other organic compounds needed for growth. Surplus carbohydrates may be stored as starch in leaves, roots, stems, seeds or other storage organs.

Food manufactured in photosynthetic tissues can also be transported to other parts of the plant. Roots, developing fruits and young growing regions often depend on this supply.

Importance of Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis provides the organic matter that forms the foundation of most food chains. Herbivores obtain food from plants, while carnivores obtain food from animals that ultimately depend on plant production. Photosynthetic organisms also contribute oxygen to the atmosphere.

Photosynthesis is therefore important for both food production and the maintenance of atmospheric oxygen.

Photosynthesis and nutrition are not interchangeable terms. Photosynthesis is the food-manufacturing process used by photosynthetic autotrophs. Nutrition is the broader process of obtaining and using nutrients.

Prelims focus

  • Green plants perform autotrophic nutrition by photosynthesis.
  • Carbon dioxide and water are the main inorganic raw materials.
  • Chlorophyll captures light energy; it is not itself a raw material consumed to form glucose.
  • Carbohydrates store chemical energy obtained through photosynthesis.
  • Starch is a common storage form of carbohydrates in plants.
  • Trap: Plants obtain mineral nutrients from soil, but manufacture most of their organic food through photosynthesis.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.2.1, printed pp. 81–82, reprint 2026–27; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 1, Nutrition in Plants, Sections 1.1–1.2, printed pp. 1–4, 2018–19 reprint; OpenStax, Biology 2e, Section 8.1, Overview of Photosynthesis, consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Autotrophic Nutrition and the Importance of Photosynthesis

body:
Why Leaves Are the Main Photosynthetic Organs

Leaves are usually the principal organs of photosynthesis because they are adapted to capture sunlight, exchange gases with the atmosphere and receive water through the plant's transport system.

The broad, flattened portion of a typical leaf is called the lamina. Its large surface helps expose photosynthetic tissues to light. Veins running through the leaf contain vascular tissues that connect it with the stem and roots.

Chloroplasts and Chlorophyll

Many cells inside the leaf contain small organelles called chloroplasts. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are the principal sites of photosynthesis in green plants.

Chlorophyll is a pigment that absorbs light energy. It is especially important in the initial energy-capturing stage of photosynthesis.

Chlorophyll is not the same as a chloroplast. A chloroplast is a cell organelle, whereas chlorophyll is a light-absorbing pigment found within it.

Leaf Cells and Gas Exchange

The internal photosynthetic tissue of a typical leaf is called the mesophyll. Its cells contain chloroplasts, and spaces between cells permit gases to move through the leaf.

Tiny openings called stomata occur in the epidermis, the outer covering of the leaf. Carbon dioxide can diffuse through these openings into the leaf. Oxygen and water vapour can diffuse out.

Stomata are commonly numerous on the lower surface of many terrestrial leaves, although their distribution varies among plant species.

Chloroplast: Organelle where photosynthesis occurs.
Chlorophyll: Pigment that captures light energy.
Stoma: Pore that enables gas exchange and water-vapour loss.

How the Raw Materials Reach the Leaf

Carbon Dioxide from the Atmosphere

Carbon dioxide enters the leaf mainly through stomata. It then diffuses through internal air spaces and reaches photosynthetic cells, where its carbon is incorporated into organic compounds.

Water from the Soil

Terrestrial plants obtain most of their water through roots. Fine extensions of root epidermal cells, known as root hairs, greatly increase the surface area available for absorption.

Absorbed water travels from roots to stems and leaves through xylem. The xylem forms part of the vascular system of the plant.

Mineral Nutrients

Plants also require mineral nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, magnesium and iron. These substances are absorbed from the soil in suitable dissolved forms and are essential for manufacturing proteins, pigments and other cellular materials.

For example, nitrogen is needed to manufacture proteins and nucleic acids. Magnesium is a constituent of chlorophyll.

Atmospheric nitrogen is abundant, but most plants cannot directly use nitrogen gas. They generally obtain usable nitrogen compounds from the soil. Certain microorganisms, including nitrogen-fixing bacteria associated with leguminous plants, help convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that can enter biological nutrient cycles.

Can Photosynthesis Occur Outside Green Leaves?

Photosynthesis is not restricted to leaves. Green stems and branches containing chloroplasts can also manufacture food. In many cacti, leaves are reduced to spines and the green stem carries out most photosynthesis.

A leaf that appears red, brown or purple is not necessarily incapable of photosynthesis. Other pigments can conceal its green chlorophyll. If suitable chloroplasts and the required conditions are present, such a leaf may photosynthesise.

Similarly, photosynthesis occurs in many green algae, not only in land plants.

The organ capable of photosynthesis is identified by its photosynthetic cells and pigments, not simply by whether it is called a leaf or appears bright green.

The Connection Between Nutrition and Transport

Photosynthesis requires materials obtained from different locations. Carbon dioxide comes mainly from the surrounding air, while terrestrial roots absorb water and minerals from the soil. The products manufactured in photosynthetic tissues must then reach other cells.

This creates 2 closely connected transport requirements: movement of water and minerals through xylem, and movement of manufactured organic food through phloem.

Prelims focus

  • Chloroplasts are the principal photosynthetic organelles in green plants.
  • Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
  • Stomata facilitate gas exchange.
  • Root hairs increase the absorptive surface area of roots.
  • Xylem supplies water and dissolved minerals to leaves.
  • Trap: Non-green-looking leaves and green stems may contain functioning photosynthetic tissues.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.2.1 and Figure 5.1, printed pp. 81–84, reprint 2026–27; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 1, Nutrition in Plants, printed pp. 1–5, and Chapter 11, Transportation in Animals and Plants, Section 11.3, printed pp. 128–131, 2018–19 reprint; OpenStax, Biology 2e, Section 8.1, Basic Photosynthetic Structures, consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Leaves, Chlorophyll and the Raw Materials Used in Photosynthesis

body:
The Main Events of Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is not a single instantaneous chemical reaction. It consists of connected processes through which light energy is captured and used to manufacture organic compounds.

At the school level, the process can be understood through 3 essential events.

  1. Absorption of light energy: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
  2. Conversion of light energy: The absorbed energy is converted into chemical energy, and water molecules are split during the light-driven reactions.
  3. Formation of carbohydrates: Carbon dioxide is incorporated into organic compounds and ultimately used to manufacture carbohydrates.

These events are connected, but they need not always occur one immediately after another. Certain drought-adapted plants can take up carbon dioxide at night and use the stored carbon compounds during daylight.

The Light-Dependent Stage

In the light-dependent reactions, chlorophyll and associated molecules capture light energy. This energy supports reactions that produce chemical energy carriers used in the next stage.

Water is split in the process, contributing electrons and hydrogen ions to the photosynthetic system. Oxygen is released as a result.

The oxygen released during oxygenic photosynthesis comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.

The Carbon-Fixation Stage

Carbon fixation means incorporating carbon from inorganic carbon dioxide into organic compounds. The Calvin cycle is the main pathway by which this fixed carbon is processed into carbohydrate precursors in photosynthetic plants.

The carbon-fixation reactions use chemical energy supplied by the light-dependent reactions. They do not directly require light at the instant each reaction occurs, but their continued operation normally depends on products generated using light.

For this reason, the older expression dark reaction can be misleading. It does not mean that plants ordinarily manufacture all their carbohydrates only at night.

Why Plants Store Starch

Photosynthesis produces carbohydrate compounds that can be converted into glucose and other sugars. When these carbohydrates are not immediately required, plants may convert part of the surplus into starch.

Starch is an insoluble storage carbohydrate. It enables plants to retain food reserves that can later be broken down and used for respiration, growth or other functions.

What Starch Formation Indicates

The appearance of starch in a previously starch-depleted, illuminated green leaf provides evidence that carbohydrates have been manufactured through photosynthesis.

Observations using illuminated and non-illuminated leaf regions show the importance of light. Comparisons involving green and non-green regions help demonstrate the role of chlorophyll. Comparisons involving carbon dioxide availability show that carbon dioxide is required for normal photosynthetic carbon fixation.

These observations support the underlying requirements of photosynthesis. They do not mean that every living leaf always contains a large, easily detectable starch reserve.

Photosynthesis and Respiration Are Different Processes

Photosynthesis stores energy in organic compounds. Cellular respiration releases usable energy from organic compounds so that cells can perform essential activities.

FeaturePhotosynthesisCellular respiration
Main functionManufactures organic compounds using light energyReleases usable energy from organic compounds
Principal location in green plantsChloroplastsPrimarily mitochondria, with initial steps in cytoplasm
Light requirementDepends on light energyDoes not directly require light
OccurrenceWhen suitable photosynthetic conditions existContinues in living cells during day and night
Overall carbon effectIncorporates carbon dioxide into organic matterOrdinarily releases carbon dioxide during aerobic breakdown of carbohydrates

Green plants therefore carry out both photosynthesis and respiration. During daylight, photosynthesis may consume more carbon dioxide than respiration releases, producing a net uptake of carbon dioxide. At night, when photosynthesis is not taking place, respiration continues.

Photosynthesis manufactures energy-rich organic compounds; respiration releases energy from such compounds. A plant does not stop respiring when sunlight becomes available.

Prelims focus

  • Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
  • Light-dependent reactions involve the splitting of water and release of oxygen.
  • Carbon fixation incorporates carbon dioxide into organic compounds.
  • The Calvin cycle is associated with carbohydrate formation.
  • Starch is a storage carbohydrate produced from photosynthetic products.
  • Trap: Light-independent reactions are not necessarily night-time reactions, and plants respire during both day and night.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, Life Processes, Section 5.2.1, printed pp. 81–84, reprint 2026–27; NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Chapter 11, Photosynthesis in Higher Plants, Sections 11.5–11.7 and 11.7.2, printed pp. 138–145, reprint 2026–27; OpenStax, Biology 2e, Section 8.1, Overview of Photosynthesis, consulted 4 November 2026.]
